missed_issues: Apart from risk labels, the reviewer-side comparison is empty. Missing-evidence detection, placeholder detection, contributor-confirmation status and gate state are coded 'not applicable / not observable' for all 37 ordinary-material outputs (Tables S38-S39). So §7.6's claim that AGM 'improved ... missing-evidence recognition, gate-state judgment, and accountability visibility' has no comparison arm. The one outcome measured in both arms, 'governance state correct', was 36/37 ordinary vs 38/38 AGM (Table S36), which is essentially no difference.

The audit's cue rates (4% evidence-obligation, 10% risk-classification, 14% review-support, 12% machine-readable cues) and the 0/50 'project-wide arrangement' result come from the three-tier recoding. That recoding was done after the legacy AI-governance variables reached kappa 0.000, 0.000, 0.000, 0.444, -0.216 and 0.167 on the 15-repo check (Table S10), and no reliability check of the new strata is reported. Only the artifact-presence figures (58% agent instruction file, 40% AGENTS.md) have shown inter-coder agreement.

The ordinary arm contains a finding that does not depend on the circular AGM comparison. Agent-assisted reviewers given only a diff, PR description and test output under-classified risk in 22/37 outputs and over-classified in none. In 11/37 the label was two or more levels below the reference. The authentication/dependency task was under-classified in 6/8 and the CI-workflow task in 7/7, while the documentation task was correct in 7/7 (Tables S36-S37). The scale is the authors' own, but the direction is one-sided.

Untagged P16: AGM 'evidence' is test commands and results written by the contributor's agent. The deterministic validator checks that command and result fields exist and are not placeholders (§S7 validation rule, Table S25), but it does not re-execute anything. A fabricated passing result therefore validates, and S8 concedes AGM is not 'an anti-fraud guarantee'. The reviewer-side gains rest on trusting self-reported evidence.

Contributor-side confirmation changed no content in any of 45 tasks; only the stage and confirmation fields moved from draft to final (§7.5, S7). The authors read this as role separation working, but it is equally what rubber-stamp confirmation looks like (compare 2607.08885, where programmers accepted incorrect assertions they had reviewed). Task C also told participants that maintainer review must stay pending, so the boundary was instructed, not discovered.

The controlled demo repository and its checks are Python (demo_app/auth.py, python -m pytest; Table S25), and all five reviewer tasks are author-built changes to that one demo. No JVM or multi-repository case is examined.
note: I agree with the review's verdict, its COI call and every pattern stance; my blind scores differ by at most one point. Its weak grades on risk-label recovery and perceived support are right, because only the AGM arm was given the risk-zone rules and labels. The review was slightly harsh in two places. Reproducibility merits 3 rather than 2, since the artifact is public, pinned to commit c781a2f, and ships deterministic scripts and a pytest suite. And the ordinary arm's one-sided under-classification of authentication, dependency and CI-workflow changes is a usable finding, not just 'people find a label when written down'. It missed that the evidence, gate and confirmation outcomes have no comparison arm at all, that the recoded audit strata have no reliability check, and that agent-written test evidence is never re-executed.
